spots.name: Pashupatinath Temple
spots.label: Pashupatinath

text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot; navigate to the Pashupatinath temple area on the Bagmati River by map. The temple is about 44 metres to the north-east of that point. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.geographic_location: Pashupatinath stands on the banks of the sacred Bagmati River in Kathmandu. Steps on the eastern bank face the aarati platform.
text.access_note: This is a working place of worship and a World Heritage precinct: photography is not allowed inside the main sanctum and non-Hindus cannot enter it, so check the official site before you go for current visiting and ticket rules.
text.description:
Pashupatinath is a Hindu temple to Pashupati, a form of Shiva, set on the banks of the Bagmati River. It is one of the oldest and most important religious complexes in South Asia, and part of the Kathmandu Valley UNESCO World Heritage listing since 1979. The main temple is a Newari-style pagoda with copper roofs covered in gold and a gold pinnacle, about 23 metres tall. It stands among hundreds of smaller shrines (518 mini-temples) across a precinct of 246 hectares. The temple is recorded as early as 400 CE, and its present form dates from a renovation in 1692.

The view works because one frame can hold the golden roofs, the river and the stone ghats (the bathing and ritual steps along the water). From the stone steps on the eastern bank facing the aarati platform (often called Arya Ghat), you can frame the temple's roofs together with the river, the ghats and the evening ceremony. Guides treat the eastern bank as the best all-round angle. The hilltop Pashupatinath Viewpoint is a good alternative if you want a slightly higher, wider look over the complex, its roofs, the river and the valley.

This is a living place of worship, so photograph with care. Keep your distance from mourners and from any cremation, never use flash near the rites, and leave drones at home.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the gold roof to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the gold keeps its detail and the sky does not wash out. For the evening ceremony, hold the phone steady against your body or a rail and let night mode work if the app offers it. A Live Photo can catch the movement of the ceremony. Do not use flash.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, roughly 3:30 to 5:00 PM, when the light falls on the golden roof. Stay on for the evening aarati.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the roofs on an upper third, with the river and ghats filling the lower part. Keep the steps or the water's edge in the foreground to give a sense of depth. For a wider, higher view of the whole complex, try the Pashupatinath Viewpoint on the hill as an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the roofs, river and ghats into one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the golden roofs. The ultra-wide (0.5x) suits the steps and the crowd in the foreground, but the temple will look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Arya Ghat (east bank of the Bagmati, on the stone steps facing the aarati platform). The temple's golden pagoda roofs across the river, with the ghats and the evening aarati in the foreground.

spots.alt: Pashupatinath Temple, Kathmandu: a Hindu temple to Pashupati. Photo spot

spots.name: Swayambhunath
spots.label: Swayambhunath

text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops near here; the site lies west of central Kathmandu. The long staircase from the east leads straight up to the main platform. A road also runs around the hill from the south to the south-west entrance. From the phone icon on the map the subject is right beside you, so there is no extra walk once you are on the terrace. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.geographic_location: Swayambhunath stands on a hill in the Kathmandu Valley, west of Kathmandu city. The stupa is on the hilltop and the city and valley spread out below it.
text.access_note: This is an active place of worship and a World Heritage Site where an entrance fee may apply and some areas may be closed after earthquake damage, so check the official site before you go.
text.description: Swayambhunath sits on top of a hill west of Kathmandu city, and it is an ancient Buddhist and Hindu pilgrimage site in the Kathmandu Valley. The white dome carries a cube painted with the Eyes of Buddha, which look out in all four directions. Above the cube are thirteen gold-plated rings that stand for the stages before nirvana. The hill is also home to families of monkeys, which is why many people call it the Monkey Temple. It photographs well because the eyes, the gold spire, the prayer flags and the valley below all fit into one climb. The stupa was renovated in May 2010, its first major renovation since 1921, and re-gilded with 20 kg of gold. It was damaged in the April 2015 earthquake, so some areas may be closed. UNESCO listed the site in 1979. Pratap Malla built the long eastern stairway in the seventeenth century, and a long staircase from the east leads directly to the main platform. The most popular shot is from the upper terrace on the northeast/east side of the dome, looking back across the valley. The gilded spire and Buddha eyes fill the foreground and the valley opens out below. For a second angle, try the World Peace Pond, where the gilded statue stands in the pool with the climb behind it. Maha Manjushree Temple gives a wider view of the whole hilltop. Go early if you can, as morning light falls on the eastern face and haze builds later.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the Buddha eyes to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the gold and white do not burn out against the sky. Take a few frames, as flags and visitors keep moving. Check for no-photography signs before shooting inside any shrine, and ask before photographing worshippers.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before haze builds up, when the sun lights the eastern face. Clear views of the Himalaya are seasonal, mainly October to February.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the Buddha eyes on an upper line, with the valley filling the lower part of the frame. Keep the spire upright by lining it up with a vertical gridline. For a wider, calmer view of the whole hilltop complex, try Maha Manjushree Temple as an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the dome and spire with some of the valley behind. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole terrace, flags and view together. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the Buddha eyes and the gold rings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Look back toward the valley, with the gilded spire and Buddha eyes in the foreground and the Kathmandu Valley spread out below.

spots.alt: Swayambhunath, Kathmandu: an ancient Buddhist and Hindu pilgrimage site in the Kathmandu Valley. Photo spot

spots.name: Garden of Dreams
spots.label: Garden of Dreams

text.directions_text: No nearby stops are listed for this spot, so start from Thamel, which is right next to the garden, and head toward the former Royal Palace side of the area. The garden is in Kaiser Mahal on Tridevi Sadak, near Thamel and Kantipath, so you can navigate to it by name: the Garden of Dreams (Kaiser Mahal). Once inside, the phone icon on the map is in the middle of the garden at the central pond. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.geographic_location: The Garden of Dreams is in Kaiser Mahal, on Tridevi Sadak in central Kathmandu. It lies across the street from the former Royal Palace, at the entrance to the Thamel tourist area and near Kantipath.
text.access_note: This is a ticketed garden, so check the official site before you go for current entry rules, restrictions on photography equipment and any closed areas.
text.description:
The Garden of Dreams is a calm, walled garden tucked into the busy streets near Thamel. It was laid out in 1920 as a private garden for Field Marshal Kaiser Sumsher Rana and designed by Kishore Narshingh. The look is Edwardian in spirit: neat, straight lines of pavilions, pergolas, urns and balustrades set against softer, more natural planting. Around 6,895 square metres of garden remain, with three pavilions, an amphitheatre and several ponds. After decades of neglect it was restored between 2000 and 2007, and it is now open to visitors.

It photographs well because everything is arranged around the paths and water, so the garden gives you ready-made frames. The classic shot is from the central lotus pond, looking back toward the pavilions, with the buildings and flower beds reflected in the water. Use the paths as leading lines and let the pavilions sit in the upper half of the picture, with their reflection below.

Two other good frames are inside the garden. At Barkha Pavilion, let the architecture fill the background and put a person in the foreground. At the Open Air Theatre, frame the curved seating against the greenery. Keep your phone steady on a railing or low wall rather than relying on a tripod. Check the official site before you go, as some rules and closed areas may apply.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pavilions to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out. Hold the phone as still as you can for sharp reflections, and keep the lens clean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the water is still enough to reflect the pavilions.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the water's edge on the lower third line, so the pavilions and their reflection balance. Let the pathways lead the eye into the picture. For an alternative, fill the frame with Barkha Pavilion and put a person in front of it, or frame the curved Open Air Theatre against the trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the pond view, which covers the pavilions and their reflection in one frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavilions are cut off, and use telephoto (2x-5x) to pick out details such as an urn or pergola.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you look back toward the pavilions, with the pond, the surrounding pavilions and the flower beds reflected in the water, framed by the pathways. For a different view, try Barkha Pavilion or the Open Air Theatre.

spots.alt: Garden of Dreams, Kathmandu: a calm, walled garden tucked into the busy streets near Thamel. Photo spot
